Among various FPGA-based designs, the Deep Learning Processor Unit (DPU) released by Xilinx has become a popular choice for accelerating CNN inference. However, the standard toolchain for the Xilinx DPU supports only the deployment of homogeneous DPU architectures, which limits flexibility and resource utilization for multi-task workloads. This paper introduces RT-DPU, a systematic approach for the automated deployment of heterogeneous multi-DPU engines on FPGAs. Our method aims to meet real-time deadlines for a set of CNN inference tasks while minimizing FPGA fabric resource consumption. First, we develop a performance model that captures the combined impact of DPU compute capacity, resource usage, and CNN model characteristics. Based on this model, we propose a heuristic-based scheduling algorithm that partitions CNN tasks into segments and maps them to appropriate DPUs, reducing response times and balancing utilization. We further introduce an automated architecture selection algorithm to identify the optimal mix of heterogeneous DPU types for a given workload. We evaluate RT-DPU on a Xilinx ZCU102 platform. Experimental results demonstrate that RT-DPU consistently meets all task deadlines while reducing BRAM consumption by up to 34.6% compared to conventional homogeneous DPU baselines. Moreover, RT-DPU successfully schedules task sets that homogeneous deployments fail to complete within their timing constraints.
author: Hai Ren, Yunlong Yu, Wei Zhang, Zelin Du, Zili Shao, Nan Guan, Lei Ju

title: W2HP: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Multi-Domain Service Function Chain Deployment
content: As network function virtualization (NFV) expands across administrative boundaries, multi-domain service function chain placement (MD-SFCP) faces a critical dilemma: achieving global optimization requires sharing sensitive topology information, while domain autonomy mandates strict privacy protection. Existing solutions typically fall into two extremes: constructing a quasi-global view via heavy state exchange, which compromises privacy and scalability, or relying on independent multi-agent learning that optimizes intra-domain placement (Where) but neglects the critical domain-selection decision (Which). Consequently, these methods fail to explicitly evaluate domain-level capabilities prior to node-level assignment, leading to load imbalance and resource inefficiency. To bridge this gap, we propose W2HP, a Which-and- Where Hierarchical Placement framework. W2HP employs an information-isolated centralized-distributed architecture, where each domain retains its fine-grained local state and exposes only an encoded domain representation to the high-level central agent for domain selection, thereby avoiding direct exchange of raw intra-domain resource states. Inside domains, low-level agents execute fine-grained node placement. We design a dual-encoder network to process hierarchical states and utilize Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) with a centralized critic to stabilize cooperative training. Extensive experiments on three network scales demonstrate that W2HP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving the acceptance ratio by up to 8.3% in large-scale scenarios and increasing the revenue-to-cost ratio by 12.26%, proving its efficacy in balancing cross-domain coordination with local autonomy.
author: Peiying Zhang, Shengpeng Chen, Chunming Rong, Ching-Hsien Hsu, Neeraj Kumar, Mohsen Guizani

title: RTHeterSim: A Simulator for Real-Time Task Scheduling on Heterogeneous Computing Platforms
content: The rising popularity of AI applications is driving the adoption of heterogeneous computing architectures to handle complex computations. However, as these systems increase in complexity, designing and optimizing runtime scheduling for multiple tasks under strict timing constraints becomes increasingly challenging. In addition, validating strict timing guarantees requires significant time and engineering effort. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a comprehensive hierarchical simulation methodology and a corresponding simulator, RTHeterSim, for runtime scheduling on configurable heterogeneous platforms. The simulator supports both idealized and statistically calibrated hardware models, whether off-the-shelf or customizable, and allows execution of both independent and dependency-constrained tasks. We verify the simulator’s timing behavior against real systems in both micro and macro perspectives. Utilizing this tool, we present three practical applications that were previously time-consuming but now readily achievable: 1) Estimate the real-time schedulability of heterogeneous hardware configurations during pre-silicon architecture design phase, guiding hardware architecture design decisions; 2) Leverage reinforcement learning to develop new scheduling strategies at the scheduler design stage, improving throughput compared to classical schedulers; and 3) Optimize the timing-safe DVFS by scanning the scheduling timeline, at deployment optimization stage, to further enhance power and energy efficiency.
author: Yinchen Ni, Yuankai Xu, Jiace Zhu, Yehan Ma, Wei Yan, Tianrui Ma, Weidong Cao, An Zou

title: HyGra: Accelerating Network-State Simulation for LLM Training in DCNs via Adaptive Packet-Flow Granularity
content: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have driven substantial intelligent transformation across diverse industries. Commercial LLM training is typically performed over data center networks (DCNs) comprising hundreds to thousands of GPUs, with multiple devices collocated per node. As network scale expands, inter-node communication becomes a primary bottleneck to training efficiency. Network-state simulators therefore play a crucial role by enabling cost-effective evaluation of network configurations and parallelization strategies through faithful emulation of DCN dynamics during LLM training. However, existing simulators are constrained by an efficiency-fidelity trade-off, as packet-level simulators (PLSs) incur prohibitive runtime overhead, whereas flow-level simulators (FLSs) compromise essential modeling accuracy. In this paper, we develop HyGra, a hybrid-granularity network-state simulator that exploits intrinsic network dynamics in LLM training to adaptively switch simulation granularity. Specifically, HyGra employs packet-level simulation during non-steady phases with transient fluctuations and flow-level simulation during steady phases with periodic patterns, thereby accelerating execution while preserving high fidelity. Moreover, it requires no specialized hardware, supports single-machine deployment, and is compatible with existing simulators. Experiments based on representative commercial LLM workloads, including ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Qwen, show that HyGra achieves up to 15.4× speedup under single parallelization strategy and 7.8× under hybrid parallelization strategies while maintaining high accuracy.
author: Wenyi Wang, Zheng Wu, Yanmeng Wang, Haolin Mao, Lei Han, Weibei Fan, Gaogang Xie, Fu Xiao

title: Exploring SLO-Aware GPU Function Overselling in Multi-Tenant FaaS Platforms
content: Serving ML models with serverless computing has become increasingly popular in recent years. Many of today’s cloud vendors have provided GPU functions to meet the performance requirements of different ML scenarios. However, existing production FaaS platforms suffer from GPU under-utilization and high cloud costs due to poor GPU resource management. In this paper, we propose gShare, an on-demand, efficient GPU function management policy for FaaS platforms. gShare provides a fine-grained GPU virtualization solution for a VM-based multi-tenant FaaS environment. It further decouples the GPU resource from the existing CPU-oriented function management paradigm, enabling flexible GPU sharing across tenants. With a dynamic and SLO-aware GPU overselling policy design, gShare can safely improve the cost-efficiency of GPU functions without causing perceptible user-side performance degradation. Experimental results show that gShare can reduce GPU usage by 43%–63% compared to the baseline while meeting more than 95% of user latency targets. Compared with the state-of-the-art method, it can also reduce cloud costs by 24%-58% while maintaining better function performance, benefiting both the cloud provider and users.
author: Yanan Yang, Zhengxiong Jiang, Meiqi Zhu, Hongqiang Xu, Yujun Wang, Liang Li, Jiansong Zhang, Xiaoyao Huang, Yiming Li, Jie Wu

title: Exploiting Product Codes for Efficient Wide Stripe Generation With Repair Efficiency Guarantee
content: Large-scale storage systems rely on erasure coding to achieve cost-effective data redundancy by storing stripes of data and parity blocks across multiple clusters. To meet the evolving storage demands, modern storage systems adopt wide stripes for extreme storage savings. Particularly, stripe merging which merges small-sized stripes into larger ones can be applied to generate wide stripes. However, this process incurs high cross-cluster network traffic due to parity block recalculation, and negatively impacts the post-merging repair efficiency by increasing the stripe width and cross-cluster transfers for single-block repairs. In this paper, we exploit Product Codes (PCs) to enable efficient wide stripe generation in hierarchical, cluster-based storage systems. Building on a hierarchy-aware repair design that leverages column-based and row-based codes to facilitate inner-cluster repairs while ensuring tolerance to cluster failures, we propose a corresponding hierarchy-aware design for stripe merging. We formalize two distinct stripe merging problems specific to PCs. We further co-design the data placement and encoding matrices of the stripes to be merged, localizing the stripe merging process within clusters. We implement hierarchy-aware PCs in a distributed storage prototype and show that our scheme significantly reduces the stripe merging and repair times compared to other hierarchy-aware erasure coding schemes.
author: Chaoqun Li, Si Wu, Jinyao Liu, Feng Li, Pengfei Hu

title: AutoNet: A Two-Stage Router Configuration Recommendation Framework Integrating Structured Semantic Modeling and Constraint Solving
content: Network configuration recommendation suggests subsequent commands and parameters while operators write, modify, or troubleshoot configurations. A practical recommender must understand command hierarchy, support heterogeneous vendor syntax, use manual knowledge, check topology and protocol constraints, and maintain low latency during interactive configuration authoring. This paper proposes AutoNet, a two-stage router configuration recommendation framework that integrates structured semantic modeling and constraint solving. AutoNet uses a semantic intermediate representation to describe command hierarchy, contextual relationships, and parameter placeholders, where a schema token denotes a configuration keyword or a normalized parameter placeholder in the structured command schema. AutoNet introduces three designs: (1) semantic intermediate representation and configuration knowledge graph construction, which organize command hierarchy, contextual features, and manual knowledge; (2) LLM-based schema-token prediction, which ranks the next configuration keywords or parameter placeholders under the current configuration context; and (3) constraint-based parameter solving, which generates and ranks concrete parameter candidates under topology, vendor-manual, and user-defined constraints. Experiments on multi-device configuration datasets show that AutoNet achieves approximately 93% end-to-end Top-1 and 95.7% Top-5 recommendation accuracy, while strict site-disjoint splits maintain 99.2–99.4% schema-token accuracy. The Z3-based parameter solver runs in sub-millisecond time for individual parameter calls, and independent rule-based CLI/protocol validation confirms high compliance with encoded syntax and protocol checks.
author: Chunyuan Liu, Zhengxin Hua, Fuliang Li, Lei Yang, Qiang He, Xingwei Wang, Jiannong Cao

title: LazyDM: A Machine Learning-Empowered Hot Data Management to Mitigate Premature Migration in High-Density Hybrid SSDs
content: Modern high-density flash memory technologies, such as Quad-Level Cell (QLC), commonly employ a hybrid architecture in which a subset of QLC blocks operates in Single-Level Cell (SLC) mode as a cache for the remaining QLC blocks. In this architecture, hot data is initially programmed to the SLC cache and later migrated to the QLC region at block-level granularity. However, limited SLC cache capacity and coarse migration granularity can cause hot data that has not yet cooled to be prematurely migrated to the QLC region, significantly degrading SSD performance and lifespan. This phenomenon is referred to as premature migration. To address this issue, this study proposes LazyDM—a machine learning-based hot data management for SLC cache, designed to optimize both performance and reliability in high-density hybrid SSDs. In particular, we develop a machine learning model to predict the duration over which data remains hot (referred to as hotness duration). We devise a hot data allocation scheme that segregates data in the SLC cache based on their hotness durations, ensuring that hot data within each block exhibit comparable cooling times. We further introduce a cooling-aware data migration scheme that efficiently relocates cooled data from the SLC cache to the QLC region, thereby preventing the performance degradation and endurance reduction caused by premature migration. Experimental results show that, compared with state-of-the-art techniques, our LazyDM reduces the hot data migration ratio, average read response time, average write response time, number of garbage collections (GCs), and number of valid page migrations by an average of 55.14%, 15.82%, 23.19%, 21.97%, and 42.83%, respectively. In addition, LazyDM improves the SLC read hit ratio by an average of 19.34%.
author: Peng Zhou, Yuhui Deng, Yi Zhou, Jiande Huang, Qifen Yang, Zhen Zhang, Lin Cui, Xiao Qin

title: Adapting Microservice Deployment at Network Edge via Distributed Graph Reinforcement Learning
content: Microservice (MS) architecture breaks down an application into lightweight service modules, making it an ideal choice for delivering complex applications in resource-constrained mobile edge computing (MEC) networks. This paper studies an Edge Micro-Service (EdgeMS) platform with a specific focus on EdgeMS deployment. EdgeMS deployment refers to installing MS modules at geo-distributed edge servers and enables cross-site function calls to accomplish the full functionalities. This problem is particularly challenging due to the implicit impact of disunified platform configurations, the complicated interactions of MS modules over dynamic MEC networks, and the deployment coupling across edge servers. We propose a novel algorithm called Distributed Graph Reinforcement Learning (DGRL) to handle the above unique challenges. DGRL employs a reinforcement learning framework that learns an EdgeMS deployment policy by directly interacting with the EdgeMS platform, thereby avoiding inaccurate characterizations of various influencing factors under disunified platform configurations. DGRL embeds graph neural networks as its learning engine, enabling it to capture complicated interactions between MS modules over dynamic edge networks. Particularly, DGRL designs a novel mechanism to realize distributed inference and training of GNNs, making it possible to generate site-wise deployment policies and drastically improve scalability for coupled decision-making. We evaluate the performance of DGRL on a realistic MEC network topology, utilizing real-world MS applications, and compare it against state-of-the-art learning strategies in both centralized and distributed settings. The results demonstrate that DGRL reduces the data transmission delay and computing delay 24.58× and 10.19×, respectively, during learning, while maintaining performance comparable to centralized learning. Additionally, DGRL exhibits superior scalability compared to federated learning.
author: Lixing Chen, Zhongqi Miao, Yang Bai, Pan Zhou, Zhe Qu, Jianhua Li, Cailian Chen

title: GSlider: A Cloud Gaming Framework Enabling Fine-Grained and Flexible Offloading
content: Cloud gaming has gained significant popularity by offloading computation and rendering to cloud servers while streaming video to thin clients. However, the rising GPU demands of modern games pose challenges, including high server costs and potential quality of service issues under heavy workloads. Recent research explores hybrid approaches, such as partial rendering offloading to clients, but existing solutions lack flexibility, either overburdening clients or underutilizing their resources. This paper introduces GSlider, a novel framework that dynamically combines video and graphics streaming. By splitting the screen into adjustable portions rendered separately on the server (video stream) and client (graphics stream), GSlider enables proportional workload offloading based on client capabilities and system conditions. The key advantages of GSlider include: (1) adaptive offloading for optimal resource use, (2) real-time adjustments to workload distribution, and (3) compatibility with unmodified games based on the Direct3D rendering pipeline. Experiments using real games show GSlider reduces latency by up to 42%, improves frame rates by up to 76%, and reduces server GPU utilization by up to 50% while maintaining high visual quality (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) $\mathbf{\gt}$> 37 dB).
author: Zhongshu Cheng, Yusen Li, Xiaoguang Liu, Gang Wang

title: Towards High-Throughput and Low-Latency Heterogeneous Blockchains via RL-Driven Network Sharding
content: Sharded blockchains enable scalable distributed ledgers by partitioning transaction workloads into multiple parallel processing shards. However, existing sharding protocols for heterogeneous blockchain environments mainly focus on mitigating performance degradation caused by uneven node bandwidth, while overlooking dynamic network variations, such as bandwidth fluctuations, unstable packet delivery, and transaction queue accumulation. These factors result in inefficient shard utilization and significant performance disparities among shards. To address these issues, we propose PabShard, an intelligent sharding framework for heterogeneous blockchain systems. PabShard leverages reinforcement learning to adaptively regulate shard operations according to network states and workload conditions. Specifically, we address two key challenges. First, to achieve effective shard organization under heterogeneous network conditions, we design a PPO-driven shard control mechanism that dynamically adjusts shard configurations based on observed system states. Meanwhile, an asymmetric bandwidth-adaptive asynchronous Merkle tree (BA-AMT) is introduced to improve transaction verification efficiency by exploiting available bandwidth resources. Second, to alleviate transaction congestion caused by heterogeneous shard processing capacities, we develop an adaptive block generation rate control mechanism that dynamically regulates the processing capability of individual shards. We implement PabShard on a Huawei Cloud cluster with heterogeneous bandwidth configurations ranging from 20 to 60 Mbit/s, where each physical host supports numerous virtualized blockchain nodes. Extensive experiments against representative sharding protocols, including Monoxide, GearBox, and Manifoldchain, demonstrate the effectiveness of PabShard. Under a transaction arrival rate of 3000 TPS with eight shards, PabShard achieves a 12.3% throughput improvement and reduces confirmation latency by 14.8% compared with the best-performing baseline.
author: Juncheng Ma, Baochao Chen, Changzhi Li, Weilian Xue, Xiulong Liu, Hongtao Xiao, Abdulnanzar G. Gulomsafdarov, Haipeng Yao, Liehuang Zhu, Keqiu Li

title: PopDedup: Defending Against Malicious Cloud Behavior in Popularity-Based Encrypted Deduplication
content: Encrypted deduplication eliminates duplicate encrypted data, reducing storage costs while preserving data privacy. Popularity-based encrypted deduplication provides different levels of protection for data according to the number of owners to balance security and performance. Most existing schemes rely on a trusted third party, which is unrealistic in many scenarios. Recently, Ha et al. (TDSC’24) propose a scheme that eliminates the need for a trusted third party. However, their approach is vulnerable to smuggle attacks (SAs) and popularity-faking attacks (PFAs) caused by malicious cloud behavior. In this paper, we propose PopDedup, a popularity-based encrypted deduplication scheme aimed at thwarting malicious cloud behavior and improving system performance. First, we integrate homomorphic encryption (HE) and digital signatures to devise unforgeable random tags for recording data popularity to prevent SAs. Second, we develop a verifiable popularity detection method to ensure the correctness of popularity detection, thereby thwarting PFAs. Third, we implement pre-selection of popular data based on unbalanced private set intersection (PSI) to enhance performance. Finally, we employ HE to present a proof-of-ownership (PoW) scheme to provide resistance against popularity tamper attacks (PTAs). Security analysis and performance evaluation demonstrate that PopDedup offers stronger security guarantees with limited overhead compared to existing schemes.
author: Guanxiong Ha, Xiaowei Ge, Chunfu Jia, Zhen Su, Rongxi Wang

title: RTMSSD: A Racetrack Memory Based Page-Level Storage Architecture for Fast and High-Reliable Persistency
content: Current SSDs employ various expensive optimization algorithms, e.g., garbage collection (GC), wear leveling (WL), and out-of-place updates, to solve the issues such as limited device life and write amplification. Indeed, they still struggle to bridge the performance gap between host and storage due to the time-consuming erase operation of NAND flash. As a magnetic storage, Racetrack Memory (RTM) performs tape-like access with longer endurance and fast write, making it a potential persistent storage medium. However, there are still three challenges when applying RTM to the general persistency architecture. (1) Traditional three-layer space management model, i.e., block-page-sector, introduces a large number of redundant operations under RTM context. (2) The current fault-tolerant mechanism in SSDs cannot solve the position errors in RTM persistency. (3) The read-first strategy in SSDs cannot benefit from the fast write of RTM. In order to solve the above problems, we propose RTMSSD, a architecture for RTM-based persistent storage. (1) The page-level storage architecture accurately manages pages access and performs fast address translation without mapping table. (2) The fault-tolerant mechanism for RTM persistency uses encoding and rewriting to achieve commercial-level reliability. (3) The new transaction scheduling method prioritizes error correction while ensuring balance between read and write. Experiments show that, comparing to SSDs, the end-to-end latency of RTMSSD can be reduced to 26% on average. In addition, compared with the corresponding RTM-based storage configurations without fault tolerance, the PAECC method proposed in this work improves the simulated Mean Time to Failure (MTTF) by approximately four orders of magnitude even in the worst evaluated case, making RTM-based storage approach the reliability level required for commercial use.
author: Jihe Wang, Xiaoyan Wang, Lin Chai, Zhiying Zhang, Danghui Wang, Bing Guo

title: In-Storage Heterogeneous Acceleration For Scalable Long-Read Mapping
content: Near-data processing accelerates data-intensive applications by moving computation closer to data, reducing data movement overhead and improving performance and efficiency. This paradigm is particularly promising in genome analysis, where read mapping, a critical step for aligning DNA sequences to reference genomes, poses substantial challenges due to the sheer volume and complexity of the data. Traditional software solutions and high-performance computing (HPC) clusters struggle with the rapid growth of genomic datasets, while specialized hardware accelerators remain limited by data movement. In this paper, we present Mendel, a heterogeneous near-storage architecture for end-to-end long-read mapping that combines storage-side, memory-side, and FPGA-based acceleration within an SSD-centered design. Mendel features a superscalar chunk-based pipeline and a chunk-aware filtering heuristic, specifically designed to handle long DNA sequences. Under our modeling-, simulation-, and synthesis-based evaluation, Mendel outperforms the long-read hardware mapper Darwin by up to 2.97${\boldsymbol{\times}}$× in performance and 17.97${\boldsymbol{\times}}$× in energy efficiency. Compared with Darwin enhanced with GenStore-style in-storage filtering, Mendel also provides higher projected performance and lower projected energy consumption in our evaluated setting.
author: Stefano Mercogliano, Kangqi Chen, Can Firtina, Taha Shahroodi, Haiyu Mao, Mohammad Sadrosadati, Alessandro Cilardo, Onur Mutlu

title: Ruler: Extremely Efficient Power-Aware Optimization for Latency-Critical Systems
content: Latency-critical applications (LC apps) deployed in data centers continuously process user requests while meeting strict tail latency constraints. Therefore, servers typically operate at low loads and maintain high CPU frequencies to meet tail latency targets, leading to significant energy waste. However, optimizing server energy consumption while maintaining tail latency constraints for LC apps is extremely challenging, requiring coordinated optimization of dynamic and static energy consumption. Therefore, we designed a Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling method, Ruler, which achieves power optimization through dynamic $\boldsymbol{Px}$Px Tailtable construction and an asymmetric frequency control strategy with protection mechanisms. Furthermore, leveraging fine-grained power optimization capabilities of Ruler, we designed its extension method, RulerDuo, a method for multi-threaded LC apps. Request aggregation is implemented based on dynamic thread sleep, thereby stably optimizing the C-state of idle cores. Finally, our method was validated under real-world load conditions using a real dataset, demonstrating that it achieves optimal power efficiency while realistically meeting tail latency constraints.
author: Huikang Huang, Weiwei Lin, Xiaoxuan Luo, Xiumin Wang, Keqin Li

title: PALM: Protocol-Aware PCIe Link Fault Prediction for Large-Scale GPU Clusters
content: As the backbone of GPU cluster interconnection, PCIe links play a critical role in supporting large-scale AI parallel computing, and their failures can trigger communication stalls, job interruptions, or even large-scale training failures. However, prior studies have primarily focused on individual-device fault prediction or system-level post-failure diagnosis, leaving PCIe link fault prediction underexplored. This task faces several unique challenges: PCIe self-recovery obscures early fault signals, topology-level fault propagation decouples the root cause from the symptoms, and firmware/driver updates cause telemetry distribution shifts. These challenges are difficult to address using telemetry signals alone and require the model to understand PCIe protocol behavior. To this end, we propose PALM, a Protocol-Aware prediction framework powered by Large Language Models. It is built upon two core engines: a Sentinel Engine, which develops a Granger-causality model to filter protocol noise and a state signature extractor to identify fault signatures; and an Arbiter Engine that translates these signatures into diagnostic evidence via a protocol-guided VLM, then fuses this evidence through an NN–VLM co-refinement predictor for reliable prediction. This detect-then-arbitrate pipeline bridges anomaly detection and protocol-level reasoning, grounding predictions in protocol semantics. Evaluated on Alibaba Cloud production data, PALM achieves 2.45$\mathbf{\times}$×, 7.91$\mathbf{\times}$×, and 6.60$\mathbf{\times}$× the average Precision, Recall, and F1-score of the five SOTA baselines, respectively.
author: Yangfan Li, Zeyu Li, Zhaoyuan Zhang, Mengquan Li, Junyu He, Fan Xu, Fengxiao Tang, Kenli Li

title: Feather: A Two-Phase Propose-and-Endorse Consensus Protocol for Asynchronous Blockchains
content: BFT-like consensus protocols have two drawbacks: i) their three-phase synchronization latency is high, and ii) the communication overhead among consensus nodes is high. Consequently, we are motivated to design a lightweight consensus that enables low-communication asynchronous operations. To this end, we present a new consensus protocol, Feather, which is lightweight and enables asynchronous blockchains. Feather employs a two-phase propose-and-endorse consensus that uses a unique mechanism in which only a subset of nodes (i.e., proposers) participate in block generation asynchronously. Compared with BFT-like protocols, Feather can dramatically reduce the communication overhead and the state-synchronization latency. This is because Feather can achieve fast local approximate consensus across multiple asynchronous consensus zones, effectively eliminating forks. To demonstrate the practicality of Feather protocol, we implement a prototype using Golang and deploy it in two types of environments: i) a local deployment over 13 local high-performance physical machines, and ii) a global deployment of 100 cloud virtual machines across 10 global cities. The experimental results show that Feather achieves $\mathbf{2.5\times}$2.5× and $\mathbf{7.3\times}$7.3× higher transaction throughput than improved PBFT and Algorand.
author: Xiaofei Luo, Jian Zheng, Huawei Huang, Zhaokang Yin, Guang Ye, Bin Xiao

title: DCO: Dynamic Cache Orchestration for LLM Accelerators Through Predictive Management
content: The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) is pushing AI accelerators toward increasingly powerful and specialized designs. Instead of further complicating software development with deeply hierarchical scratchpad memories (SPMs) and their asynchronous management, we investigate the opposite end of the design spectrum: a multi-core AI accelerator equipped with a shared system-level cache and application-aware management policies, while keeping the programming effort modest. Our approach exploits dataflow information available in the software stack to guide cache replacement (including dead-block prediction), in concert with bypass decisions and mechanisms that alleviate cache thrashing. We evaluate the proposal using a cycle-accurate simulator on FlashAttention-based LLM workloads and observe substantial performance gains—up to 1.90× speedup over a conventional LRU-managed LLC across a range of cache sizes and dataflows. In addition, we build and validate an analytical model that takes into account the actual overlapping behaviors to extend the measurement results of our policies to real-world larger-scale workloads. Experimental results show that when functioning together, our dead block prediction, bypassing, and thrashing mitigation strategies can handle scenarios both with and without inter-core data sharing and achieve remarkable speedups. Finally, we implement the TMU in RTL using Chisel and synthesize it in a 15 nm standard-cell library: the TMU occupies only $\mathbf{0.064mm^{2}}$0.064mm2 and can operate at 2 GHz. Our findings demonstrate that a shared system-level cache, when coupled with lightweight tensor-aware orchestration, is a practical and scalable alternative to deeply hierarchical software-managed SPMs in future AI accelerator systems.
author: Zhongchun Zhou, Chengtao Lai, Yuhang Gu, Wei Zhang

title: Computing Without Learning: An Information-Theoretically Secure Multiparty Evaluation of Deterministic Pushdown Automata
content: Multiparty computation allows a finite group of parties to jointly compute a known function of their combined inputs without revealing any individual’s input. This work presents a multiparty computation protocol for evaluating a private string on a deterministic pushdown automaton. The protocol takes as input both the automaton’s description and the string, and ensures that no party learns either the automaton or the string; they only learn whether the automaton accepts or rejects the string. This study emphasizes three main contributions. First, is it possible to compute a private function among a finite set of parties, where no party learns either the function or the inputs? We show that the answer is affirmative for computational models like pushdown automata. Second, our protocol provides a general framework for evaluating deterministic pushdown automata, thereby classifying a subclass of context-free languages that can be evaluated privately using multiparty computation. Finally, the proposed work is secure under the information-theoretic paradigm and inherently quantum safe.
author: Soumen Sarkar, Jaydeep Howlader

title: A Delay Optimization Approach for Ternary HS-FPRM Logic Circuits Based on a Goal-Driven Hierarchical Multi-Task Optimization Framework
content: Logic synthesis is a critical step in integrated circuit design, where delay optimization of ternary logic circuits has become one of the key challenges. However, the delay optimization for ternary Fixed Polarity Reed-Muller (FPRM) logic circuits is an NP-hard problem. Therefore, we propose a novel paradigm of a ternary Hierarchical Structure-based FPRM (HS-FPRM) logic expression using the divide-and-conquer strategy. Each hierarchical level corresponds to a distinct ternary FPRM logic circuit. By integrating hierarchical logic circuits at the gate level, a complete ternary HS-FPRM logic circuit is constructed. However, the delay optimization for ternary HS-FPRM circuits is a complex nested combinatorial optimization problem. To address this problem, we propose a Goal-Driven Hierarchical Multi-Task Optimization (GD-HMTO) framework. First, this framework integrates a goal-driven dynamic task partitioning strategy to adaptively refine the hierarchical structure. Second, it incorporates a hierarchical optimization with an inter-task interaction mechanism. This mechanism simultaneously searches for the optimal polarity corresponding to minimal delay across all levels. Finally, a task-specific intensive optimization strategy is applied to prevent local traps. Furthermore, based on the proposed multi-level parallel Huffman tree delay decomposition model compatible with multi-valued programmable logic array characteristics, we propose a delay optimization approach for a ternary HS-FPRM logic circuit with the minimum delay using the GD-HMTO. Experimental results on the Microelectronics Center of North Carolina Benchmark test circuits indicate that the proposed delay optimization approach shows effectiveness and superiority compared to the state-of-the-art delay optimization approaches.
author: Xiaoqian Wu, Peng Wang, Huaxiao Liu, Lei Liu

title: Enabling Distributed Cooperative Full-Size LLM Inference With Tensor Parallelism Across Heterogeneous Edge Devices
content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly penetrating various fields, enhancing a wide range of tasks and services. Enabling edge devices for LLM inference can benefit real-time applications for end users. However, resource limitations and heterogeneity over edge devices hinder the deployment of the full-size LLM. In this paper, we propose a novel LLM inference system in edge environments, facilitating cooperative inference across low-profile edge devices. The system incorporates tensor parallelism technologies across heterogeneous devices, addressing challenges related to limited resources and asynchronous operations in such scenarios. We formulate the problem as a convex integer optimization problem to determine optimal partition strategies. We propose solutions with theoretical bounds on the optimal value. We conduct extensive experiments with real edge devices and large-scale numerical simulations to assess the performance of the proposed solutions. Results from experiments and simulations demonstrate that our approach achieves efficient model partitioning and up to 0.65 seconds per token for full-size model inference performance in edge environments.
author: Yaodong Huang, Weixuan Peng, Yi Guo, Lin Zhu, Laizhong Cui

title: Optimal Grouping for K-Indistinguishable Data Accesses in Encrypted KV Stores
content: With the explosive growth of data, many users are outsourcing their local private data to cloud servers for encrypted key-value storage. However, recent research has revealed that even with pre-encryption, attackers can still deduce sensitive information by analyzing the access frequency patterns of key-value pairs. To mitigate this issue, some studies propose sending additional dummy queries to smooth access frequency. However, the access frequencies of key-value pairs typically vary greatly in practice, and these methods can significantly increase the bandwidth overhead of user queries. A viable strategy is to partition key-value pairs into different data groups, thereby smoothing frequencies in each group to prevent attackers from distinguishing key-value pairs in a group. Based on this idea, we designed an optimal grouping scheme for encrypted $\boldsymbol{KV}$KV stores to achieve $\boldsymbol{K}$K-indistinguishable data accesses with the minimum bandwidth cost, called $\boldsymbol{K}$K-Opt. The scheme employs a dynamic programming algorithm to partition data into groups, each containing at least $\boldsymbol{K}$K key-value pairs. To address dynamic workloads, we further introduce an online processing scheme for dynamic data operations, which ensures security and low overhead while efficiently handling insertions, deletions, and updates. In addition, we conduct a comprehensive security analysis of the proposed scheme and implement it in Redis. Experimental results show that $\boldsymbol{K}$K-Opt achieves the optimal grouping structure in the static setting and reduces bandwidth overhead compared with existing baselines, while maintaining low overhead under dynamic workloads.
author: Qiuyu Hu, Xijie Ba, Qin Liu, Zhenyu Chai, Xiaohong Li, Peng Li

title: Symphony: A Sharded Blockchain for Efficient Smart Contract Execution
content: Sharding is a promising approach to increase blockchain throughput by partitioning the system into multiple shards and distributing the workload. However, existing sharded blockchains exhibit poor performance in executing cross-shard smart contract transactions, which require costly multi-round consensus and heavy cross-shard communication to synchronize data. Furthermore, as the system scales with more shards, the volume of cross-shard transactions naturally increases, thereby impeding the scalability of the entire system. In this paper, we present Symphony, a sharded blockchain designed for efficient smart contract execution. Symphony offloads cross-shard smart contract transactions to Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), where stateless EVMs perform off-chain execution to bypass multi-round consensus, significantly accelerating processing. To ensure security and liveness, Symphony introduces enclave pools that provide redundancy for these off-chain executions. Additionally, Symphony integrates a Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based account allocation algorithm to reduce the cross-shard interaction ratio while preserving workload balance across shards. We evaluated our prototype using real-world Ethereum mainnet workloads. The results show that Symphony improves throughput by 36% and reduces latency by 40.8% compared to LightCross.
author: Rongkai Zhang, Qiuyu Ding, Qianyi Liu, Shengjie Guan, Jing Shi, Zhen Xiao, Mingchao Wan, Changrui Ren, Jin Dong

title: Gemini: An Online Mitigation System Against Sneaky DoS Attacks in SDN
content: An architecture known as software-defined networking abstracts a network’s many levels, which increases agility and flexibility but also raises security concerns. In this paper, we discuss a low-rate DoS attack, called sneaky DoS attacks. This attack achieves its goal by sending instantaneous high-rate traffic at regular intervals, triggering TCP congestion control mechanisms. The attack features a low average rate and a high instantaneous rate. SDN architecture offers fresh concepts for defensing online attacks. We propose an online mitigation system Gemini for sneaky DoS attacks. It can monitor and defend the attacks in real-time. Monitor module uses dynamic thresholds to measure fluctuations of traffic. Detection module collects traffic features and detects sneaky DoS attacks. Mitigation module uses three LN-norms to measure the similarity of sequences, and calculate suspicious scores. After locating attack sources based on suspicious scores, we send flow rules to drop attack packets. The result shows that Gemini is a lightweight system, and it can accurately detect and mitigate Sneaky DoS attacks within an average of 9 seconds.
author: Dan Tang, Ran Tao, Chenjun Gao, Keqin Li, Zheng Qin, Jiliang Zhang, Rui Dai

title: Holistic Orchestration of Resource Reservation for Reducing Operation Costs in Geo-Distributed Cloud
content: Cloud providers establish datacenters across zones interconnected by backbone network lines, in which the zones and network lines differ in compute and network cost efficiency. For the resource availability of large tenants, cloud providers typically reserve sufficient computing and network resources for them. To reduce the operation cost of cloud providers, current orchestrators focus solely on reducing compute or network costs. However, optimizing one resource type may obviously increase the cost of another. We propose a holistic orchestration scheme Merkur to reduce compute and network costs for resource reservations. Merkur formalizes the holistic orchestration as an optimization model and step-by-step reduces the compute and network costs by: fine-grained orchestrating, network peak shaving, and low-cost zone filling. The orchestrating strategy orchestrates computing and network resources across zones hourly. The shaving strategy reduces the monthly network bandwidth reservations to reduce network costs. The filling strategy reserves more computing resources to zones with lower compute costs. Experiments show Merkur reduces the overall operation cost by 19.3% on average, compared to state-of-the-art geo-distributed orchestrators.
author: Jiuchen Shi, Zhixin Tong, Quan Chen, Kaihua Fu, Liwei Song, Pengfei Huang, Yinuo Li, Mosong Zhou, Mingliang Yin, Deze Zeng, Xiaohua Tian, Minyi Guo

title: Addressing Hard Problems of Cache Coherence Protocols Verification Through Enhanced Directed Model Checking
content: Cache coherence protocols are essential in multi-core industrial processor systems. However, their increasing complexity, particularly due to the numerous rules involved in each protocol transaction, results in an exponentially expanding state space. Traditional model checking techniques, such as Murphi, demonstrate limitations in addressing this complexity. For instance, TileLink Cached (TL-C) coherence protocols, widely implemented in RISC-V open-source processors, exemplify these verification difficulties. To tackle the deep target states arising from complex protocol transactions, we design a new directed model checking framework combined with random walk. Additionally, we introduce a novel scoring function to efficiently guide the search process by leveraging variable dependencies within cache protocols. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our search framework and scoring function.
author: Kun Ma, Yongjian Li, Kaifan Wang, Yongxin Zhao, Shaowei Cai

title: DIFCVerilog: Decoupling Capabilities and Taints for Fine-Grained Information Flow in Hardware
content: Modern System-on-Chip designs extensively integrate third-party IP cores, many from untrusted sources, increasingly facing threats of information theft and malicious injection from hardware Trojans. Although information flow tracking (IFT) can detect illegal information flows, it often requires manual annotation of leakage points beforehand, making it easy to miss sinks that are carefully disguised by Trojans and causing false negatives. Static information flow isolation security is mainly based on formal verification, but requires extensive manual marking and has limited scalability. This paper combines IFT with the verification of dynamic security policies, and proposes DIFCVerilog, a hardware description language for static information flow verification with dynamic label semantics. It introduces capability inheritance and taint propagation mechanisms to adapt to dynamic risk boundaries of information flow, enabling automated detection of policy-violating information flows after the required security policies, module capabilities, and initial taint annotations are provided. For verification, we constructed an automated analysis framework based on Prolog predicate logic, mapping hardware designs to logical predicates, and modeling taint propagation and path evolution through fixed-point iteration to complete detection without hardware execution. We formally define the type system and operational semantics of DIFCVerilog and establish non-interference for well-typed programs under the core language semantics (see Supplementary Material). Experimental results show that DIFCVerilog effectively detects the evaluated malicious-injection and information-leakage vulnerabilities while maintaining practical analysis efficiency and scalability on the evaluated large designs.
author: Yubo Shi, Zhi Yang, Shuyuan Jin, Bingren Wu

title: A System-Level Exploration of Superconducting Supercomputers for Emerging Workloads
content: Superconducting digital (SCD) technology has long carried promise for advancing large-scale computing leveraging the unique physical characteristics of superconducting materials and devices, such as low-voltage, high-frequency operation and zero-resistance interconnects. At the same time, SCD technology has also historically been beset with many scaling challenges. However, recent critical advances including improved power delivery, high integration density and availability of superconducting random-access memory prompt a fresh evaluation of SCD-based computing. In this paper, we study whether SCD systems can outperform conventional CMOS and cryo-CMOS for large-scale workloads even after accounting for full system overheads. Using a novel multilevel analytical modeling framework, our study explores performance implications of various SCD configurations across a range of architecture and technology assumptions in applications such as large language models (LLMs). The results show that, despite cooling overheads, a key benefit of recently proposed SCD technology is 9$\boldsymbol{\times}$× - 286$\boldsymbol{\times}$× better energy efficiency. By contrast, performance gains ranging between 4$\boldsymbol{\times}$× - 16$\boldsymbol{\times}$× are more limited and strongly depend on the availability of high-density, high-bandwidth on-chip memory that traditionally was not attainable. In general, the results show that recent technological advances are key to a promising scalable path forward, where our ablation studies highlight critical aspects of the maturity of SCD technology.
author: Daniel Peralta Velazquez, Siyuan Ma, Sairam Sri Vatsavai, Saikat Chakraborty, Lingda Li, Anna Herr, Manu Perumkunnil Komalan, Quentin Herr, George Biros, Jaydeep Kulkarni, Lizy Kurian John, Andreas Gerstlauer

title: CacheFly: Adaptive in-Network Cache Coordination for Distributed Key-Value Storage Systems
content: Distributed key-value (KV) storage systems serve as the infrastructure for latency-sensitive cloud services, yet they frequently suffer from severe load imbalance caused by highly skewed and fast-evolving workloads. Existing in-network caching designs rely on static cache placement, while host-level blocking data migration introduces heavyweight overhead and service disruption, making such approaches incapable of handling rapid hotspot shifts efficiently. This paper presents CacheFly, an adaptive in-network cache coordination framework for distributed KV storage, which enables adaptive and non-disruptive cache reallocation across Top-of-Rack (ToR) switches. CacheFly adopts a hybrid architecture that decouples line-rate data plane operations from control plane global load analysis and spine-layer routing updates. Transfer cache responsibility among switches through lightweight metadata exchange, avoiding expensive host-level blocking data migration, and preserve data consistency during ownership transitions by strictly serializing writes and filtering stale state-synchronization traffic in the data plane. We implement a full-stack prototype on Intel Tofino programmable switches with DPDK-accelerated Redis backends. Extensive evaluations show that CacheFly sustains near-optimal throughput under extreme Zipfian workloads, eliminates rack-level load imbalance, and scales smoothly with cluster size.
author: Xianda Meng, Ammar Hawbani, Jiangyuan Chen, Mohammad Qatawneh, Ahmed Al-Dubai, Liang Zhao

title: A Multi-Attribute-Based Fault Diagnosis Framework for Hypercube-Based Networks
content: Driven by the accelerated advance in high-performance computing (HPC) and cloud computing paradigms, the connectivity and diagnosability of multiprocessor systems under the $\boldsymbol{h}$h-extra $\boldsymbol{r}$r-component strategy ($\mathbf{(}\boldsymbol{h,r}\mathbf{)}$(h,r)-ECDS), which requires that the residual network contains at least $\boldsymbol{r}$r connected components, each holding at least $\boldsymbol{h+1}$h+1 nodes, were proposed to address the urgent need for efficient fault diagnosis in complex interconnection networks with multi-attribute fault pattern. As two key metrics for fault tolerance and reliability of interconnection networks within the $\boldsymbol{(h,r)}$(h,r)-ECDS, the $\boldsymbol{h}$h-extra $\boldsymbol{r}$r-component connectivity and $\boldsymbol{h}$h-extra $\boldsymbol{r}$r-component diagnosability primarily concentrate on possible scenarios in which the eradication of a faulty node set induces a residual network with only a few connected components, each owning a certain number of processing units. In this paper, we investigate the metric relationship between $\boldsymbol{h}$h-extra $\boldsymbol{r}$r-component connectivity $\boldsymbol{c}\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\boldsymbol{h}}\boldsymbol{(G)}$cκrh(G) and $\boldsymbol{h}$h-extra $\boldsymbol{r}$r-component diagnosability $\boldsymbol{ct_{r}^{h}(G)}$ctrh(G) under PMC model, i.e., $\boldsymbol{ct_{r}^{h}(G)=c\kappa_{r+1}^{h}(G)+h}$ctrh(G)=cκr+1h(G)+h. Furthermore, we determine the connectivity and diagnosability under the $\boldsymbol{(h,r)}$(h,r)-ECDS for a class of networks $\mathcal{G}$G for $\boldsymbol{h=1}$h=1 and $\boldsymbol{r\geq 2}$r≥2. Subsequently, we extend the application of this metric to various networks, such as hypercube, half hypercube, hierarchical cubic network, bicube network, hierarchical hypercube network, exchanged hypercube and dual cube. In addition, we suggest a diagnosis algorithm, PSDCGD-PMC, tailored for efficiently identifying faulty nodes under the $\boldsymbol{(h,r)}$(h,r)-ECDS. Leveraging parallel submodule-based divide-and-conquer strategies, the proposed algorithm shows outstanding performance in handling large-scale networks. On popular interconnection network (hypercube), small-world network (Watts-Strogatz network) and real-world network (BCSSTM12), our experimental results validate their superior performance, with high precision metrics confirming both efficiency and accuracy.
author: Yifan Li, Shuming Zhou, Sun-Yuan Hsieh, Kaiyue Meng

title: GPBchain: A GNN-Assisted Framework for Optimizing Sharding Blockchain Reconfiguration
content: Blockchain is widely regarded as the foundational infrastructure for Web3. However, its inherent scalability limitations hinder its ability to support large-scale Web3 applications. Sharding technology is one of the most promising approaches to deal with the scalability problem by partitioning accounts into separate shards and allowing each shard to handle a portion of transactions (TXs) in parallel. However, this approach inevitably introduces cross-shard TXs (CSTs), and minimizing CSTs while maintaining inter-shard workload balance remains a challenging trade-off, preventing system throughput from scaling linearly with the number of shards. Existing solutions typically employ heuristic graph partitioning methods during the sharding blockchain reconfiguration phase to reduce CSTs and balance workload across shards. Nevertheless, these methods are often sensitive to parameter settings, exhibit limited generalizability, and struggle to adapt to the rapidly evolving TX patterns. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised sharding blockchain framework based on Graph Neural Network (GNN) called GPBchain, which achieves explicit joint optimization of CST reduction and inter-shard workload balancing. During the reconfiguration phase, GPBchain leverages GNN for account reallocation, taking into account both the ratio of CSTs and inter-shard workload balancing to optimize account distribution. Compared with existing solutions, experimental results conducted on the real Ethereum on-chain data illustrate that GPBchain achieves superior joint optimization of CST reduction and inter-shard workload balancing, thereby enhancing the overall throughput of sharding blockchain systems.
author: Kaimin Zhang, Xingwei Wang, Bo Yi, Min Huang, Lin Qiu

title: Speeding up Dynamic CPU Allocation in Linux
content: CPU allocation, and CPU pinning in particular, allows to assign CPU cores to an application. In Linux, the assignation of physical cores to a group of processes (an application) is done statically at creation time. An affinity mask is assigned to the parent process, and this mask is inherited automatically by its children. The problem is that changing at runtime the affinity mask for a group of processes is an inefficient operation. It requires 1) to enumerate all the involved processes in the group—which may be easy if you are the programmer of the application, but not so if its a third party application—, and 2) to execute one system call to change the mask on each process. In this paper we propose a solution that allows a process to share (instead of inherit) its affinity mask with its children, and therefore a single system call is required to change the affinity mask to a whole group of processes. Two implementations are developed: 1) a kernel module and 2) a direct modification of the kernel source code. Experimental results show that our proposal to change the affinity mask of an application with a low number of processes performs the same as the current implementation, while changing a high number of processes (a hierarchy of 500 processes) gets a maximum of 32x speedup (when all the children PIDs are known). And when the list of children is unknown—and they must be retrieved from the /proc directory—results in a maximum of 600x speedup.
author: Xavier López, Juan José Costa, Yolanda Becerra

title: An Effective Q-Learning Unified Memory Prefetching System Based on Deep Neural Networks
content: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are increasingly becoming wider and deeper, which consequently limits their training performance due to GPU memory constraints. To break the GPU memory wall in scaling deep learning workloads, CUDA Unified Memory (UM) has emerged as a widely adopted framework that allows memory oversubscription through a page fault mechanism. However, page migration often introduces more overhead, which decreases memory performance and training efficiency. In this paper, we propose Q-learning-based Unified Memory Prefetcher (QUMP), a memory management method to optimize the memory migration process. QUMP uses Q-learning algorithm to interact with the task processing state of GPU kernels and determines the prefetching policy that can maximize the accuracy of memory migration. We verified the performance of QUMP through real analysis of the memory access characteristics within the GPU in actual machine experiments. Compared with traditional prefetching strategies, QUMP reduces the GPU memory usage by 6.5% without sacrificing training efficiency. Meanwhile, our QUMP-batch scheme improves the throughput by 50.3%. QUMP is implemented purely in software and requires no hardware changes. Experimental results show that QUMP outperforms common logical prefetching strategies and achieves performance and throughput improvements for DNN training.
author: Yuening Wang, Juan Fang, Ziyi Teng, Ran Zhai, Qi Ming, Neal N. Xiong

title: Sanitizable and Revocable Outsourced CP-ABE Against Internal Threats in Vehicular Networks
content: Ciphertext-Policy Attribute-Based Encryption (CP-ABE) is a cryptographic primitive for secure and fine-grained data sharing in the Internet of Vehicles (IoV). However, traditional schemes rely on the ideal assumption that data owners are fully honest. In practice, potentially malicious data owners may intentionally generate vulnerable ciphertexts or share hidden trapdoors to collude with unauthorized entities. As a result, unauthorized entities can bypass the access control system, leading to privacy leakage. To mitigate this internal threat, sanitizable access control schemes have been proposed. However, these frameworks suffer from linear parameter expansion, incur high computational and storage overheads, and only achieve Selective-CPA security. To address these limitations, we propose an efficient, sanitizable, and revocable outsourced access control scheme with Adaptive-CPA security. Constructed over Type-III pairings, our framework supports arbitrary attributes without incurring parameter expansion. This design reduces both computational and storage overheads. Experimental results show that our scheme accelerates encryption, sanitization, and total decryption by approximately 3 times, 1.7 times, and 9 times, respectively, while reducing the storage of public parameters and secret keys by over 12 times and 2 times compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, we prove that our framework achieves Adaptive-CPA security.
author: Zhi Zhang, Jiayun Yan, Qiaohan Chu, Le Zeng, Jie Chen, Debiao He

title: DPDA: A Dynamic Partition-Driven Data Allocation Scheme for Boosting Hybrid SSD Performance
content: QLC NAND flash provides superior storage density and cost-effectiveness at the expense of substantial programming latencies. To improve latency performance, hybrid SSDs incorporate high-speed SLC cache to mitigate the latency overhead of QLC flash. However, the hybrid architecture induces a critical performance bottleneck termed Hot-Write Blocking (HWB): prolonged QLC write operations monopolize flash chips, thereby stalling subsequent hot-data writes to SLC cache. This interference significantly exacerbates queuing latency and severely degrades SLC write performance. To address this issue, we propose a dynamic partition-driven data allocation scheme called DPDA that mitigates the hot-write blocking problem in hybrid architecture SSDs. DPDA partitions the parallel planes of an SSD into hot and cold partitions, and segregates hot and cold requests to the planes of distinct partitions, thereby isolating mutually interfering write streams. Specifically, the scheme implements a data dispatch module to allocate latency-sensitive hot requests to the SLC regions of planes in the hot partition, thereby shielding them from the interference of cold QLC writes. Moreover, to prevent insufficient SLC space in hot partitions, DPDA implements a partition control unit to dynamically swap the planes of hot and cold partitions by space utilization, and then uses the SLC regions of the swapped plane to serve hot requests, thus fully utilizing the SLC resources in hybrid SSDs. We compare DPDA with three state-of-the-art schemes SPA, AMPHIBIAN and RRTS in terms of write waiting time, write latency, and read latency under eight real-world workloads. The experimental results show that compared with the existing schemes, DPDA slashes the hot write waiting time, hot write latency, and average write latency by 52.99%, 51.86%, and 47.55%, respectively.
author: Junyao Chen, Shujie Pang, Yuhui Deng, Jinquan Zhang, Xiaoping Li

title: Persistent Attacks Against Nakamoto-Style Blockchains and the Efficacy of Mitigation
content: Nakamoto consensus is the most widely adopted decentralized consensus mechanism in cryptocurrency systems. Since it was proposed in 2008, many studies have focused on analyzing its security. Most of them focused on maximizing the profit of the adversary. Examples include the selfish mining attack and the recent Riskless Uncle Maker (RUM) attack. In this work, we introduce the Staircase-Unrestricted Uncle Maker (SUUM), the first block-withholding attack targeting the timestamp-based Nakamoto-style blockchain. Through block withholding, timestamp manipulation, and difficulty risk control, SUUM adversaries are capable of launching persistent, near-zero-cost attacks with minimal difficulty risk, indefinitely extracting rewards from honest participants. We conduct a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of SUUM, including its attack conditions, blockchain-level impact, and difficulty risk. We conduct an empirical analysis on three major Nakamoto-style blockchains, namely Ethereum 1.x, Ethereum Classic, and Ethereum PoW. Statistical results suggest that, as of January 2026, seven major mining pools had launched the SUUM attacks by manipulating timestamps.
author: Junjie Hu, Lanting Huang, Na Ruan

title: FlexVector: A SpMM Vector Accelerator With Flexible VRF for GCNs on Varying-Sparsity Graphs
content: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are widely adopted for tasks involving relational or graph-structured data and can be formulated as two-stage sparse–dense matrix multiplication (SpMM) during inference. However, existing accelerators often struggle with the irregular workloads induced by power-law node degree distributions. In this work, we propose FlexVector, a domain-specific vector accelerator that efficiently executes SpMM for GCN inference under irregular workloads. FlexVector adopts a row-wise, product-based dataflow that regularizes SpMM execution and exposes vector parallelism through full-row access to vector registers, eliminating the need for multi-banked register file designs. Building on this dataflow, it introduces software-managed, flexible vector register files (VRFs) that adapt to irregular data access patterns, without sacrificing memory access efficiency. To further exploit these architectural capabilities, we develop a graph preprocessing strategy that restructures irregular graph workloads to better match the row-wise dataflow and VRF capacity. This hardware–software co-design reduces memory traffic, leading to significant performance and energy efficiency gains on real-world GCN workloads. Experimental results on five real-world GCN datasets show that the VRF-centric FlexVector achieves a $\mathbf{3.78\times}$3.78× speedup and 40.5% lower energy at comparable area cost relative to a state-of-the-art cache-centric baseline with buffers of the same size.
author: Bohan Li, Shengmin Li, Xinyu Shi, Enyi Yao, Francky Catthoor, Simei Yang
